title: The question
lines: Type in a ZIP code, pick ten miles, and a store locator hands back everything nearby.
Here's what happens between that click and the list of results.

title: A ZIP becomes a point
lines: A ZIP code isn't really a place. It's a bundle of mail routes, drawn as an irregular shape.
So the first step swaps the ZIP for a single point: its centroid.
That's a latitude and longitude, looked up from a table of roughly forty thousand ZIP codes.

title: Measure everything
lines: The simplest search measures the distance from that point to every store, using the haversine formula for distance on a sphere.
It works. But it means thousands of trig calculations for every single query.

title: Box first, circle second
lines: So we cheat first. A box ten miles in each direction is just four numbers: a minimum and maximum latitude and longitude.
An ordinary database index throws out everything outside the box almost for free.
Only stores inside the box get the exact distance check, and the ones in the corners, outside the circle, are dropped.

title: Which ZIPs are nearby?
lines: Often a record only has a ZIP code, not coordinates. Then the question changes: which ZIP codes are within ten miles?
The usual answer is every ZIP whose centroid falls inside the circle.
That list goes straight into a query: where zip is in this set.

title: Centroids hide the shape
lines: But a centroid hides the shape around it.
A ZIP whose center sits just outside the circle can still reach well inside it, and it gets left out.
To reason about that, we need to know which area belongs to which point.

title: Growing Voronoi cells
lines: That's exactly what a Voronoi diagram gives us.
Let every centroid grow outward at the same speed. Wherever two growing regions meet, they stop.
Each finished cell holds every spot on the map that's closer to its centroid than to any other.

title: Edges and neighbors
lines: The boundaries aren't arbitrary. Each edge sits exactly halfway between two neighboring centroids, at a right angle to the line that joins them.
Connect every pair of neighbors and you get the Delaunay triangulation, the Voronoi diagram's twin.

title: Which ZIP is this?
lines: Cells also answer the reverse question.
Drop a pin anywhere, and the cell it lands in names its nearest ZIP centroid. That's a good guess at its ZIP code, with no boundary files at all.

title: Cells meet the circle
lines: Now lay the search circle over the cells.
Some cells sit entirely inside: definitely in. Some never touch it: definitely out.
The interesting ones straddle the edge. Counting every cell that touches the circle, instead of every centroid inside it, catches the ZIPs the simple test missed.

title: Walk the neighbors
lines: Neighbors also make the search fast.
Start from the cell under the search point. Step to its neighbors, then their neighbors, and stop wherever a cell no longer touches the circle.
The search only visits cells near the answer, never the whole country.

title: Do it ahead of time
lines: In production this is usually done ahead of time.
For every ZIP code, store the list of ZIPs within five, ten and twenty five miles.
A radius search becomes one lookup, and the exact distance check runs only on what comes back.

title: Recap
lines: So: turn the ZIP into a point. Filter cheaply with a box. Measure exactly with haversine.
And use Voronoi cells to see which areas your circle really covers.
That's a ZIP code radius search.
